author: A Robot
objectives: Identify DNA structural components: sugar-phosphate backbones, nitrogenous bases, and hydrogen bonds, and describe how they assemble into the double helix.
Apply complementary base-pairing rules, A with T and G with C, and relate these pairings to two versus three hydrogen bonds.
Explain the antiparallel orientation of DNA strands using 5'-to-3' sugar-phosphate backbone directionality.
Trace the functions of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork.
Explain why DNA replication produces a continuously synthesized leading strand and a discontinuously synthesized lagging strand with Okazaki fragments.
Articulate why DNA replication is semiconservative and predict daughter-molecule strand composition after one and two replication rounds.

modules.description: Students examine a rotating DNA double helix and zoomed callouts for backbone, bases, complementary base pairs, and hydrogen bonds.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the two sugar-phosphate backbones as the exterior helices of DNA.
Locate nitrogenous bases as inward-facing paired structures between the backbones.
Distinguish A-T pairs with two hydrogen bonds from G-C pairs with three hydrogen bonds.
instructions: Place the model on a clear tabletop surface about an arm's length away.
Use Next and Previous to move through the guided structural callouts.
Track the color-coded bases and bond markers as each feature is introduced.

components.text: DNA double helix
DNA: two strands twisted into a double helix

clips.changeMeaning: The complete double helix is shown rotating slowly so students first recognize DNA as two intertwined strands around a common axis.
clips.narration: This is DNA, deoxyribonucleic acid, represented as a double helix. Two strands wrap around a shared axis, creating a stable structure that stores genetic information.

components.text: Sugar-phosphate backbones form the exterior rails

clips.changeMeaning: Two translucent helical highlights appear over the DNA exterior to emphasize that the sugar-phosphate backbones form the outside rails.
clips.narration: The outside rails are sugar-phosphate backbones. Each backbone is made from repeating deoxyribose sugars and phosphate groups, and the two backbones spiral around the outside of the molecule.

components.text: Complementary base pairs: A-T and G-C

clips.changeMeaning: Enlarged A-T and G-C base-pair callouts appear to show that nitrogenous bases project inward and pair specifically across the helix.
clips.narration: The nitrogenous bases project inward from the backbones like the rungs of a twisted ladder. Adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine pairs with cytosine, keeping the helix at a consistent width.

components.text: A-T: 2 H bonds     G-C: 3 H bonds

clips.changeMeaning: Hydrogen bond markers appear between the enlarged pairs, contrasting the two bonds of A-T with the three bonds of G-C.
clips.narration: Adenine and thymine form two hydrogen bonds. Guanine and cytosine form three hydrogen bonds. These bond patterns help explain why the base-pairing rules are specific.

modules.description: A straightened DNA segment shows how 5' and 3' ends create antiparallel strand orientation while preserving complementary base pairing.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define 5' and 3' ends in the context of sugar-phosphate backbone directionality.
Explain why the two DNA strands run antiparallel rather than in the same direction.
Use complementary base-pairing rules to write the opposite strand in the correct antiparallel orientation.
instructions: Observe the straightened DNA ladder segment.
Compare the red and blue arrows as endpoint labels appear.
Read the example sequence from left to right while noticing opposite strand direction.

components.text:
Example:
5'-A G T C-3'
3'-T C A G-5'

clips.changeMeaning: The DNA is displayed as a straight ladder so students can focus on directional orientation without the visual complexity of helical twisting.
clips.narration: To focus on directionality, this DNA segment is shown as a straight ladder. The base pairs are still complementary, but the two backbones can now be compared side by side.

clips.changeMeaning: The upper strand arrow and 5' and 3' labels appear, establishing one strand as running left-to-right from 5' to 3'.
clips.narration: The upper strand has a 5 prime end on the left and a 3 prime end on the right. Its sugar-phosphate backbone therefore runs 5 prime to 3 prime from left to right.

clips.changeMeaning: The lower strand arrow and endpoint labels appear in the opposite direction, making the antiparallel relationship explicit.
clips.narration: The lower strand runs in the opposite direction: its 3 prime end is on the left and its 5 prime end is on the right. DNA strands are antiparallel.

components.text:
Example:
5'-A G T C-3'
3'-T C A G-5'

clips.changeMeaning: A text sequence panel appears to connect complementary base selection with the correct antiparallel notation for the opposite strand.
clips.narration: For example, a strand written 5 prime A G T C 3 prime pairs with 3 prime T C A G 5 prime. Complementarity determines the bases, and antiparallel direction determines how the strand is written.

modules.description: The replication fork is staged with helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, incoming nucleotides, and a growing daughter strand.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the replication fork as the site where parental DNA strands are separated and copied.
Describe helicase function in unwinding the double helix and separating parental strands.
Explain how single-strand binding proteins stabilize exposed templates.
Describe DNA polymerase as the enzyme that adds complementary nucleotides to a growing 3' end.
instructions: Follow the Y-shaped replication fork from the intact DNA region toward the separated arms.
Watch each enzyme appear at the location where it acts.
Note that DNA polymerase extends a daughter strand by adding nucleotides to its 3' end.

components.text: Replication fork enzymes
Replication fork: parental templates exposed

clips.changeMeaning: The Y-shaped parental DNA fork appears as the organizing spatial structure for all enzyme activities in the scene.
clips.narration: DNA replication occurs where the parental double helix opens into a Y-shaped replication fork. Each exposed parental strand will serve as a template for a new complementary strand.

components.text: Helicase unwinds and separates parental strands

clips.changeMeaning: A rotating helicase ring appears at the fork junction and shifts slightly into the fork to represent unwinding of the parental double helix.
clips.narration: Helicase sits at the fork and uses energy from ATP to separate the two parental strands. It disrupts hydrogen bonds between base pairs, opening the helix for copying.

components.text: SSB proteins stabilize exposed single strands

clips.changeMeaning: Purple SSB clusters appear on both separated strands to show stabilization of single-stranded DNA templates.
clips.narration: Single-strand binding proteins attach to the exposed templates. They prevent the strands from reannealing and help keep bases accessible for DNA polymerase.

components.text: DNA polymerase extends from a 3' end

clips.changeMeaning: DNA polymerase, nucleotide pool, and growing orange strand appear together to demonstrate template-directed 5' to 3' synthesis.
clips.narration: DNA polymerase reads the parental template and adds complementary nucleotides to the 3 prime end of the growing daughter strand. The new strand is extended only in the 5 prime to 3 prime direction.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Leading and Lagging Strand Synthesis
modules.description: A replication fork demonstrates continuous leading-strand synthesis, discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis as Okazaki fragments, and ligase sealing.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate the antiparallel fork geometry to the need for asymmetric DNA synthesis.
Differentiate continuous leading-strand synthesis from discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis.
Identify Okazaki fragments and explain DNA ligase's role in joining them.
instructions: Compare the upper and lower template arms at the same replication fork.
Watch the leading strand grow continuously with the fork.
Watch separate Okazaki fragments form on the lagging strand and then become sealed by ligase.

components.text: Leading and lagging strands
Antiparallel templates create synthesis asymmetry

clips.changeMeaning: The antiparallel replication fork is introduced as the geometric cause of different synthesis modes on the two templates.
clips.narration: Because the parental templates are antiparallel and DNA polymerase can synthesize only 5 prime to 3 prime, the two daughter strands cannot be made in exactly the same way.

components.text: Leading strand: continuous 5'→3' synthesis

clips.changeMeaning: The leading-strand polymerase appears and the upper daughter strand lengthens, showing continuous synthesis in the same direction as fork movement.
clips.narration: On the leading-strand template, DNA polymerase can move with the opening fork. The daughter strand is synthesized continuously in the 5 prime to 3 prime direction.

components.text: Lagging strand: discontinuous Okazaki fragments

clips.changeMeaning: The lagging-strand polymerase and separate Okazaki fragments appear along the lower template, showing discontinuous synthesis away from the fork.
clips.narration: On the lagging-strand template, 5 prime to 3 prime synthesis points away from the fork. DNA polymerase therefore makes short segments called Okazaki fragments.

components.text: DNA ligase seals fragments into one strand

clips.changeMeaning: DNA ligase appears near the gaps and the separated Okazaki fragments are replaced by one sealed strand to show backbone nick repair.
clips.narration: DNA ligase seals the nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone, joining Okazaki fragments into a continuous daughter strand.

modules.description: Color-coded daughter molecules show that each first-round double helix contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand, then extend the pattern to a second round.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define semiconservative replication as conservation of one parental strand in each first-round daughter helix.
Identify the composition of daughter DNA molecules after one replication round.
Predict the distribution of original parental strands after two replication rounds.
instructions: Use the color key to track original parental strands and newly synthesized strands.
Observe the first replication round producing two hybrid molecules.
Advance to the second round and count how many molecules retain an original parental strand.

components.text: Semiconservative replication
Blue = original parental strand | Orange = newly synthesized strand
Track old and new strands by color

clips.changeMeaning: The original parental DNA appears with a color key, allowing students to track old versus new strands through replication rounds.
clips.narration: Blue marks the original parental DNA strands. Orange marks newly synthesized strands. By following the colors, you can see why DNA replication is called semiconservative.

components.text: Round 1: each daughter = 1 parental + 1 new

clips.changeMeaning: The original molecule shifts upward while two hybrid daughter molecules appear below it, each with one blue parental strand and one orange new strand.
clips.narration: After one replication round, the two parental strands have separated and each served as a template. Each daughter molecule contains one original strand and one newly synthesized strand.

components.text: Round 2: 2 molecules retain original strands, 2 do not

clips.changeMeaning: Four second-round molecules appear, showing two hybrids that retain original strands and two molecules composed only of strands made during replication rounds.
clips.narration: After a second round from the original starting molecule, there are four DNA molecules. Two still contain one original parental strand, while two contain only strands synthesized during replication rounds.

components.text: Semiconservative = one template strand conserved in each new helix
Key idea: parental templates guide complementary synthesis and are inherited by daughter molecules

clips.changeMeaning: The final view keeps all products visible while the label summarizes the core definition of semiconservative replication.
clips.narration: Semiconservative means each newly formed double helix conserves one strand from a template molecule and pairs it with one newly synthesized complementary strand.
